\chapter{People, Paper, and a Book}
\label{ch:gu-people-paper-book}
\hlchaptermodality{34}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can hear and say five everyday Gujarati words for people and the things they read, and read and write one of them.}

Five words for people and the things they read enter meaning-first by ear, one lesson each; an oral checkpoint scores listening and speaking apart, paper reaches the page with signs taught before chapter 8, and an R1 return carries the chapter-24 three-place map back at its fourth spacing window.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[chhokro]{\gu{છોકરો} — hear boy}

\label{lesson:GU-C30-hear-chhokro}



\begin{quote}
Say the Gujarati words for brother and for sister. Now listen twice: \textbf{chhokro}. It means \textbf{boy} — younger than the \emph{bhāī} you already know, and ending in the masculine \emph{-o}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}chhokro\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}chhokro\textquotedblright{} twice, once slowly and once at speed
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{chhokro} mean? (\textbf{Boy.})

Source: \href{https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english-gujarati/boy}{Cambridge: boy}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[chhokrī]{\gu{છોકરી} — hear girl}

\label{lesson:GU-C30-hear-chhokri}



\begin{quote}
Say the word for boy. Now listen twice: \textbf{chhokrī}. It means \textbf{girl} — the pair of \emph{chhokro}, and this time the \emph{-o} and \emph{-ī} endings really do mark gender.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}chhokrī\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}chhokro\textquotedblright{} for boy, then \textquotedblleft{}chhokrī\textquotedblright{} for girl
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{chhokrī} mean? (\textbf{Girl.})

Source: \href{https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english-gujarati/girl}{Cambridge: girl}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[māṇas]{\gu{માણસ} — hear person}

\label{lesson:GU-C30-hear-maanas}



\begin{quote}
Say the words for boy and for girl. Now listen twice: \textbf{māṇas}. It means \textbf{person} — anybody at all, the word to use when boy or girl is not the question.
\end{quote}

Say these aloud:

\end{itemize}

\section[pustak]{\gu{પુસ્તક} — hear book}

\label{lesson:GU-C30-hear-pustak}



\begin{quote}
Say the Gujarati verb for \emph{to read}. Now listen twice: \textbf{pustak}. It means \textbf{book} — the thing a \emph{māṇas} reads, and it carries the same \textbf{st} join as \emph{namaste}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}pustak\textquotedblright{}

\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{pustak} mean? (\textbf{Book.})

Source: \href{https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english-gujarati/book}{Cambridge: book}.

\section[kāgaḷ]{\gu{કાગળ} — hear paper}

\label{lesson:GU-C30-hear-kaagal}



\begin{quote}
Say the words for book and for person. Now listen twice: \textbf{kāgaḷ}. It means \textbf{paper} — what a \emph{pustak} is made of, ending on the curled-back \emph{ḷ} you also hear in \emph{dāḷ}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}kāgaḷ\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}pustak\textquotedblright{} for book, then \textquotedblleft{}kāgaḷ\textquotedblright{} for paper
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{kāgaḷ} mean? (\textbf{Paper.})

Source: \href{https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english-gujarati/paper}{Cambridge: paper}.

\section[Practice]{Five people and things, by ear}

\label{lesson:GU-C30-people-five}



\begin{quote}
Nothing new arrives here. Say the first and the last word of the chapter before any list is read to you.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Keep two scores. \textbf{Listening} goes from sound to meaning; \textbf{speaking} goes from meaning to sound. A strong score in one cannot cover a miss in the other. \section[Practice]{Kāgaḷ reaches the page}

\label{lesson:GU-C30-kaagal}



\begin{quote}
Before anything is uncovered, say the Gujarati word for \textbf{paper}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Uncover \textbf{\gu{કાગળ}} once. Four pieces, none new: \textbf{\gu{ક}} from the doorway nine, the \textbf{\gu{ા}} stroke from the greeting, and \textbf{\gu{ગ}} and the curled \textbf{\gu{ળ}} from the forms taught before the verbs. Watch \textbf{\gu{ગ}} and \textbf{\gu{ળ}} side by side; they are the two most easily confused shapes here. Name the pieces aloud in order, then read the whole word once. This is the only word of the chapter the hand is asked for; the other four stay in the ear for now, which is the gloss-first order rather than an omission.

\subsection*{Writing — guided copy, model in view}
Keep the model in view and copy \textbf{\gu{કાગળ}} once. Repair one shape if it needs it; do not start a row.

\subsection*{Your turn — the first map at its fourth window}
The first three-place map was read and written more than eighty positions ago, which is its fourth spacing window; the river reached the page eight lessons ago, which is its second. Both rows here are cold reading.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two signs in \emph{kāgaḷ} are the easiest to confuse, and how do you tell them apart? (\textbf{\gu{ગ}} and \textbf{\gu{ળ}} — one opens to the right, the other curls back on itself.)

Source: \href{https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english-gujarati/paper}{Cambridge: paper}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{The people return at R1, and the first map at R4}

\label{lesson:GU-R30-people-five-r1}



\begin{quote}
Nothing new arrives here. Say the words for boy and for paper before anything is read to you.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\textbf{Listening} runs sound to meaning; \textbf{speaking} runs meaning to sound, exactly as they did one lesson ago.

\subsection*{Your turn — the distant band, the first map, and the house}
A \emph{māṇas} goes to the \emph{bajār}, comes back to the \emph{ghar}, and opens its \emph{bārṇũ}. The first three were introduced around position 136 and are asked for here more than eighty lessons later, which is the fourth spacing window; the four house words are at their third.

\subsection*{Writing — from sound, every model covered}
Record \textbf{writing} on its own; a 5/5 in listening cannot cover a miss here.

A \emph{māṇas} carries \emph{paisā} in a \emph{hāth}. Both reached the page more than eighty positions ago, which is the fourth spacing window.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How far after the checkpoint did this return come? (\textbf{Two lessons} — inside the first spacing window.)
